# Finite Difference Stencils (Central/Forward/Backward)


## Overview
Finite difference stencils compute the spatial gradient vector $\nabla V$ of a scalar volume field $V$ by approximating partial derivatives using discrete differences between neighboring voxel values [G]. This family solves the problem of estimating surface normals and edge strength for volume rendering without requiring analytic derivatives or precomputed gradient volumes [G]. It is distinguished from [Analytic Gradient Computation](2167-analytic-gradient-computation.md) by its reliance on discrete sampling rather than closed-form differentiation, and from [Gradient Estimation from Samples](2180-gradient-estimation-from-samples.md) by its deterministic, grid-aligned stencil structure rather than stochastic or ray-based estimation [G]. Builds on [Gradient Computation via Finite Differences](1077-gradient-computation-via-finite-differences.md).

## Shared principles
All methods in this family approximate the partial derivative $\frac{\partial V}{\partial x_i}$ at a voxel center $\mathbf{p}$ using a linear combination of scalar field values $V(\mathbf{p}_k)$ at neighboring positions $\mathbf{p}_k$ [G]. The general form is:
$$ G_i = \sum_{k} w_k V(\mathbf{p}_k) $$
where $w_k$ are weights determined by the stencil geometry and step size $h$ (voxel spacing) [G]. For isotropic grids with $h=1$, the weights are typically integers or simple fractions [G]. The gradient vector is assembled as $\nabla V = (G_x, G_y, G_z)$ [G]. Boundary handling is required when stencil neighbors fall outside the volume domain; common strategies include clamping, zero-padding, or extrapolation [G].

## Subtopics

### [Neumann Gradient](3342-neumann-gradient.md)
Estimates the gradient by fitting a plane to the 26 neighbors of a voxel, minimizing weighted mean-square error. It provides nearly isotropic gradients and reduces fringing artifacts compared to simple finite differences. Choose when smooth specular effects and robustness to rapid gradient direction changes are required.

### [Forward Difference Gradient](3362-forward-difference-gradient.md)
Estimates the derivative using the current voxel and the immediate neighbor in the positive direction along each axis. It is computationally cheaper than central differences (2 samples vs 3 per axis) but is first-order accurate and asymmetric. Choose for performance-critical applications where directional bias is acceptable or for dynamic deformations where precomputed gradients are invalid.

### [4th-Order Finite Difference Gradient](4889-4th-order-finite-difference-gradient.md)
Computes the gradient using a 4th-order accurate scheme with a wider stencil and boundary extrapolation to maintain accuracy at domain edges. It produces smoother normals for ray marching than lower-order methods. Choose when high-fidelity normals are required for Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or smooth scalar fields.

### [Gradient Selection](5889-gradient-selection.md)
A runtime dispatch mechanism that switches between Central Difference and Sobel operators based on configuration or boundary proximity. It balances computational cost against noise robustness. Choose when the input volume quality varies or when adaptive noise filtering is needed.

### [Gauss-Seidel with Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR)](6904-gauss-seidel-with-successive-over-relaxation-sor.md)
An iterative solver for the Laplace equation that implicitly computes scalar field values from boundary conditions. Unlike explicit finite difference stencils, it does not compute gradients from existing data but generates smooth fields. Choose for generating physically consistent scalar fields (e.g., temperature, pressure) rather than estimating gradients from existing density data.

### [Brick-local Gradient Estimation](8810-brick-local-gradient-estimation.md)
Computes gradients using central differences with sample coordinates clamped to the current brick's valid range. It ensures cache locality and avoids synchronization overhead in brick-based rendering. Choose for hierarchical or brick-based volume rendering where memory access patterns are critical.

### [Sobel-based Gradient Estimation](9967-sobel-based-gradient-estimation.md)
Uses a 3x3x3 convolution kernel with smoothing weights to compute gradients. It is less sensitive to noise than central differences but more expensive. Choose for noisy volume data where edge detection robustness is prioritized over computational speed.

### [Central Difference Stencils](9968-central-difference-stencils.md)
Computes the gradient using symmetric neighbors displaced by $\pm h$. It is second-order accurate ($O(h^2)$) and reduces directional bias. Choose as the default method for static volumes where accuracy and isotropy are important.

### [Sharded Gradient Computation](12597-sharded-gradient-computation.md)
Applies forward differences within local shards and explicitly bridges inter-shard boundaries for the partitioned axis. It handles multi-device partitioning of large volumes. Choose for distributed or multi-GPU volume rendering where data is partitioned along one axis.

### WENO5 Interpolation
A nominally fifth-order finite-difference WENO scheme that returns the numerical flux for interpolation [S1]. Given five input values $v_1=f(x-2dx), v_2=f(x-dx), v_3=f(x), v_4=f(x+dx), v_5=f(x+2dx)$, it returns an interpolated value $f(x+dx/2)$ such that $(f(x+dx/2) - f(x-dx/2))/dx = df/dx(x) + error$, where the error is fifth-order in smooth regions ($O(dx) \le error \le O(dx^5)$) [S1]. It includes a scaling factor `scale2` (default 1.0) and accepts five input values for the stencil [S1]. Introduced by Chi-Wang Shu, referenced in ICASE Report No 2001-11 and ICASE No 97-65 [S1].

## Background
The family encompasses standard finite difference approximations for gradient computation [G]. WENO5 was introduced by Chi-Wang Shu, referenced in ICASE Report No 2001-11 and ICASE No 97-65 [S1].
